title: Inverse of Vandermonde Matrix
theorem_text:
Let $V_n$ be the Vandermonde matrix of order $n$ given by:
$V_n = \begin {bmatrix}
  x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_n \\
  x_1^2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_n^2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
  x_1^n & x_2^n & \cdots & x_n^n
\end{bmatrix}$
Then its inverse $V_n^{-1} = \sqbrk b_n$ can be specified as:
$b_{i j} = \begin{cases}
\paren {-1}^{j - 1} \paren {\dfrac {\displaystyle \sum_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m_1 \mathop < \ldots \mathop < m_{n - j} \mathop \le n \\ m_1, \ldots, m_{n - j} \mathop \ne i} } x_{m_1} \cdots x_{m_{n - j} } } {x_i \displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne i} } \paren {x_m - x_i} } } & : 1 \le  j < n \\
\qquad \qquad \qquad \dfrac 1 {x_i \displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne i} } \paren {x_i - x_m} } & : j = n
\end{cases}$
proof_text:
First consider the classical form of the Vandermonde matrix:
$W_n = \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^{n - 1} \\
  1 & x_2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_2^{n - 1} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
  1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^{n - 1} \\
\end{bmatrix}$
By Vandermonde Determinant, the determinant of $W_n$ is:
$\displaystyle \map \det {W_n} = \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop < j \mathop \le n} \paren {x_i - x_j} \ne 0$
Since this is non-zero, by Matrix is Invertible iff Determinant has Multiplicative Inverse, the inverse matrix, denoted $B = \sqbrk {b_{i j} }$, is guaranteed to exist.
Using the definition of the matrix product and the inverse:
$\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_{k j} x_i^{k - 1} = \delta_{i j}$
That is, if $\map {P_j} x$ is the polynomial:
$\displaystyle \map {P_j} x := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_{k j}x^{k - 1}$
then:
$\map {P_j} {x_1} = 0, \ldots, \map {P_j} {x_{j - 1} } = 0, \map {P_j} {x_j} = 1, \map {P_j} {x_{j + 1} } = 0, \ldots, \map {P_j} {x_n} = 0$
By the Lagrange Interpolation Formula, the $j$th row of $B$ is composed of the coefficients of the $j$th Lagrange basis polynomial:
$\displaystyle \map {P_j} x = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_{k j} x^{k - 1} = \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne j} } \frac {x - x_m} {x_j - x_m}$
Identifying the $k$th order coefficient in these two polynomials yields:
$b_{k j} = \begin{cases}
\paren {-1}^{n - k} \paren {\dfrac {\displaystyle \sum_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m_1 \mathop < \ldots \mathop < m_{n - k} \mathop \le n \\ m_1, \ldots, m_{n - k} \mathop \ne j} } x_{m_1} \cdots x_{m_{n - k} } } {\displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne j} } \paren {x_j - x_m} } } & : 1 \le k < n \\
\qquad \qquad \qquad \dfrac 1 {\displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne j} } \paren {x_j - x_m}} & : k = n
\end{cases}$
which gives:
$b_{k j} = \begin{cases}
\paren {-1}^{k - 1} \paren {\dfrac {\displaystyle \sum_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m_1 \mathop < \ldots \mathop < m_{n - k} \mathop \le n \\ m_1, \ldots, m_{n - k} \mathop \ne j} } x_{m_1} \cdots x_{m_{n - k} } } {\displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne j} } \paren {x_m - x_j} } } & : 1 \le k < n \\
\qquad \qquad \qquad \dfrac 1 {\displaystyle \prod_{\substack {1 \mathop \le m \mathop \le n \\ m \mathop \ne j} } \paren {x_j - x_m} } & : k = n
\end{cases}$
For the general case, we observe that by simple multiplication:
$\displaystyle V_n = 
\begin {pmatrix}
\begin {bmatrix}
  x_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
  0 & x_2 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
  0 & 0 & \cdots & x_n
\end {bmatrix}
\cdot W_n
\end {pmatrix}^\intercal$
So by Inverse of Matrix Product and Inverse of Diagonal Matrix:
$\displaystyle V_n^{-1} = 
\begin {bmatrix}
  x_1^{-1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
  0 & x_2^{-1} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
  0 & 0 & \cdots & x_n^{-1}
\end {bmatrix} \cdot \paren {W_n^{-1} }^\intercal$
Let $c_{k j}$ denote the $\tuple {k, j}$th coefficient of $V_n^{-1}$.
Since the first matrix in the product expression for $V_n^{-1}$ above is diagonal:
$c_{kj} = \dfrac 1 {x_k} b_{j k}$
which establishes the result.
review_reason: Distinctness and nonzero values of the nodes are not assumed. Repeated nodes give identical columns, and a zero node gives a zero column, so the inverse need not exist.

title: Floor Function is Idempotent
theorem_text: $\floor {\floor x} = \floor x$
proof_text:
Let $y = \floor x$.
By the identity $\floor y=y$ for $0\le y<1$ when $y$ is an integer, we may set $y=\floor x$ in that identity and obtain $\floor{\floor x}=\floor x$.
review_reason: The cited form fixes integers in the interval [0,1). Knowing that floor(x) is integral does not place it in that interval. For x=2.7 it is 2.

title: Sum of r+k Choose k up to n
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \forall n \in \Z: n \ge 0: \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom {r + k} k = \binom {r + n + 1} n$
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
For all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition
$\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom {r + k} k = \binom {r + n + 1} n$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 0$ is true, as $\dbinom r 0 = 1 = \dbinom {r + 1} 0$ by definition.
This is our basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $\map P m$ is true, where $m \ge 0$, then it logically follows that $\map P {m + 1}$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^m \binom {r + k} k = \binom {r + m + 1} m$
Then we need to show:
$\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{m + 1} \binom {r + k} k = \binom {r + m + 2} {m + 1}$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{m+1}\binom{r+k}{k}=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom{r+k}{k}-\binom{r+m+1}{m+1}.$$
$$= \binom {r + m + 1} m + \binom {r + m + 1} {m + 1}$$
from the induction hypothesis
$$= \binom {r + m + 2} {m + 1}$$
Pascal's Rule
So $\map P m \implies \map P {m + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom {r + k} k = \binom {r + n + 1} n$
review_reason: Extending the sum adds the new binomial term. The subtraction gives the wrong recurrence and is inconsistent with the following Pascal step.

title: Alternating Sum and Difference of r Choose k up to n
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop \le n} \paren {-1}^k \binom r k = \paren {-1}^n \binom {r - 1} n$
proof_text:
$$\sum_{k \mathop \le n} \paren {-1}^k \binom r k = \sum_{k \mathop \le n} \binom {k - r - 1} k$$
Negated Upper Index of Binomial Coefficient
After this conversion, the sum is $(-1)^n\binom{r-1}{n}$, which is the required expression.
review_reason: Negating the upper index only transforms each summand. The argument omits evaluation of the transformed partial sum before asserting its final value.

title: Product of r Choose m with m Choose k
theorem_text: $\dbinom r m \dbinom m k = \dbinom r k \dbinom {r - k} {m - k}$
proof_text:
Consider the trinomial coefficient:
$\dbinom r {k, m - k, r - m}$
We use Multinomial Coefficient expressed as Product of Binomial Coefficients:
$\dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + k_3} {k_1, k_2, k_3} = \dbinom {k_1 + k_2} {k_1} \dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + k_3} {k_1 + k_2}$
and substitute as appropriate for $k_1, k_2, k_3$.
We have:
$$\dbinom r {k, m - k, r - m}$$
$$= \dbinom {\left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right) + k} {m - k, r - m, k}$$
$$= \dbinom {\left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right)} {m - k} \dbinom {\left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right) + k} {\left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right)}$$
Multinomial Coefficient expressed as Product of Binomial Coefficients
$$= \dbinom {r - k} {m - k} \dbinom r m$$
Similarly:
$$\dbinom r {k, m - k, r - m}$$
$$= \dbinom {k + \left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right)} {k, m - k, r - m}$$
$$= \dbinom {k + \left({m - k}\right)} k \dbinom {k + \left({m - k}\right) + \left({r - m}\right)} {\left({m - k}\right) + k}$$
Multinomial Coefficient expressed as Product of Binomial Coefficients
$$= \dbinom m k \dbinom r m$$
The result follows on equating the two expressions.
review_reason: The first factorization simplifies its last binomial to choose(r,m), although its lower index is r−k, giving choose(r,k). Equating the two printed results does not give the theorem.

title: Chu-Vandermonde Identity
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_k \binom r k \binom s {n - k} = \binom {r + s} n$
proof_text:
Assume $s=r$. Then $(1+x)^{r+s}=(1+x)^r(1+x)^r$. Expanding the two factors and reading the coefficient at $x^n$ gives
$$\binom{2r}{n}=\sum_k\binom r k\binom r{n-k}.$$
This is the desired identity.
review_reason: The proof assumes r=s and obtains the equal-exponent case. The theorem allows r and s to be different.

title: Chu-Vandermonde Identity
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_k \binom r k \binom s {n - k} = \binom {r + s} n$
proof_text:
This is a special case of Gauss's Hypergeometric Theorem:
${}_2F_1 \left({a, b; c; 1}\right) = \dfrac{\Gamma \left({c}\right) \Gamma \left({c - a - b}\right)} {\Gamma \left({c - a}\right) \Gamma \left({c - b}\right)}$
where:
${}_2F_1$ is the hypergeometric series
$\Gamma \left({n + 1}\right) = n!$ is the Gamma function.
One regains the Chu-Vandermonde Identity by taking $a = -n$ and applying Negated Upper Index of Binomial Coefficient:
$\dbinom n k = (-1)^k \dbinom {k - n - 1} k$
throughout.
review_reason: Specifying only a=−n leaves b and c and the normalization relating the summands undetermined. It also leaves the hypotheses of the stated gamma evaluation unchecked.

title: Congruence Modulo Zero is Diagonal Relation
theorem_text:
Congruence modulo zero is the diagonal relation.
That is:
$x \equiv y \pmod 0 \iff x = y$
proof_text:
Follows directly from the definition of congruence:
$x \equiv y \pmod z \iff x \bmod z = y \bmod z$
When $z = 0$ we have by definition:
$x \bmod 0 := x$
Therefore $x\bmod0=y\bmod0$ iff $x=-y$. The congruence relation is thus the diagonal.
review_reason: After substituting the convention x mod 0=x and y mod 0=y, equality of remainders gives x=y. There is no sign reversal on the second input.

title: Definite Integral of Partial Derivative
theorem_text:
Let $\map f {x, y}$ and $\map {\dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x} } {x, y}$ be continuous functions of $x$ and $y$ on $D = \closedint {x_1} {x_2} \times \closedint a b$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \frac \d {\d x} \int_a^b \map f {x, y} \rd y = \int_a^b \map {\frac {\partial f} {\partial x} } {x, y} \rd y$
for $x \in \closedint {x_1} {x_2}$.
proof_text:
Define $\displaystyle \map G x = \int_a^b \map f {x, y} \rd y$.
The continuity of $f$ ensures that $G$ exists.
Then by linearity of the integral:
$\dfrac {\Delta G} {\Delta x} = \dfrac {\map G {x + \Delta x} - \map G x} {\Delta x} = \displaystyle \int_a^b \frac {\map f {x + \Delta x, y} - \map f {x, y} } {\Delta x} \rd y$
We want to find the limit of this quantity as $\Delta x$ approaches zero.
For each $y \in \closedint a b$, we can consider $\map {f_y} x = \map f {x, y}$ as a separate function of the single variable $x$, with $\dfrac {\d f_y} {\d x} = \dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x}$.
Choose a single point $c$ between $x$ and $x+\Delta x$ at which the Mean Value Theorem holds for every function $f_y$. This gives
$$\frac{\Delta G}{\Delta x}=\int_a^b\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(c,y)\,dy.$$
As $\Delta x\to0$, $c$ tends to $x$. Continuity of the derivative on the compact rectangle gives convergence of this integral to $\int_a^b\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)\,dy$.
review_reason: The mean-value point may depend on y. For f(x,y)=yx²+(1−y)x³ on the unit square and an increment from 0 to 1, y=1 requires c=1/2 while y=0 requires c=1/sqrt(3).

title: Definite Integral of Partial Derivative
theorem_text:
Let $\map f {x, y}$ and $\map {\dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x} } {x, y}$ be continuous functions of $x$ and $y$ on $D = \closedint {x_1} {x_2} \times \closedint a b$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \frac \d {\d x} \int_a^b \map f {x, y} \rd y = \int_a^b \map {\frac {\partial f} {\partial x} } {x, y} \rd y$
for $x \in \closedint {x_1} {x_2}$.
proof_text: Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for differentiating an integral with respect to its upper limit to $\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dy$. Evaluating at the upper endpoint gives $f(x,b)$ as the derivative, which is the integral of the partial derivative in the claim.
review_reason: The upper-limit theorem applies when the upper limit is the variable of differentiation. Here b is constant and x enters only through the integrand, so evaluating at b gives no such derivative.

title: Sum of Floors not greater than Floor of Sum
theorem_text:
Let $\left \lfloor {x} \right \rfloor$ be the floor function.
Then:
$\left \lfloor {x} \right \rfloor + \left \lfloor {y} \right \rfloor \le \left \lfloor {x + y} \right \rfloor$
The equality holds:
$\left \lfloor {x} \right \rfloor + \left \lfloor {y} \right \rfloor = \left \lfloor {x + y} \right \rfloor$
if and only if:
$x \bmod 1 + y \bmod 1 < 1$
where $x \bmod 1$ denotes the modulo operation.
proof_text:
From the definition of the modulo operation, we have that:
$x = \left \lfloor {x}\right \rfloor + \left({x \bmod 1}\right)$
from which:
$$\left \lfloor {x + y} \right \rfloor = \left \lfloor {\left \lfloor {x}\right \rfloor + \left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left \lfloor {y}\right \rfloor + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rfloor$$
$$= \left \lfloor {x}\right \rfloor + \left \lfloor {y}\right \rfloor + \left \lfloor {\left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rfloor$$
Floor of Number plus Integer
Hence the inequality.
The equality holds if and only if:
$\left \lfloor {\left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rfloor = 0$
that is, if and only if:
$x\bmod 1+y\bmod 1\le1$.
review_reason: Floor of the fractional-part sum is zero only strictly below 1. At equality, for example x=y=1/2, the floor of the sum is 1 and the sum of floors is zero.

title: Sum of Ceilings not less than Ceiling of Sum
theorem_text:
Let $\left \lceil {x} \right \rceil$ be the ceiling function.
Then:
$\left \lceil {x} \right \rceil + \left \lceil {y} \right \rceil \ge \left \lceil {x + y} \right \rceil$
The equality holds:
$\left \lceil {x} \right \rceil + \left \lceil {y} \right \rceil = \left \lceil {x + y} \right \rceil$
if and only if either:
$x \in \Z$ or $y \in \Z$
or:
$x \bmod 1 + y \bmod 1 > 1$
where $x \bmod 1$ denotes the modulo operation.
proof_text:
From the definition of the modulo operation, we have that:
$x = \left \lfloor {x}\right \rfloor + \left({x \bmod 1}\right)$
from which we obtain:
$x = \left \lceil {x}\right \rceil - \left[{x \notin \Z}\right] + \left({x \bmod 1}\right)$
where $\left[{x \notin \Z}\right]$ uses Iverson's convention.
$$\left \lceil {x + y} \right \rceil = \left \lceil {\left \lfloor {x}\right \rfloor + \left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left \lfloor {y}\right \rfloor + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rceil$$
$$= \left \lceil {\left \lceil {x}\right \rceil - \left[{x \notin \Z}\right] + \left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left \lceil {y}\right \rceil - \left[{y \notin \Z}\right] + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rceil$$
$$= \left \lceil {x}\right \rceil + \left \lceil {y}\right \rceil + \left \lceil {\left({x \bmod 1}\right) + \left({y \bmod 1}\right)} \right \rceil - \left[{x \notin \Z}\right] - \left[{y \notin \Z}\right]$$
Ceiling of Number plus Integer
Take the two fractional parts to be equal, with common value $t\in[0,1)$. The ceiling correction is $\lceil 2t\rceil-2[t>0]$, which is nonpositive. It is zero precisely when $t=0$ or $2t>1$. Hence we obtain the stated inequality and equality criterion.
review_reason: The argument imposes equal fractional parts. The theorem includes pairs such as x=1/4 and y=1/2, whose fractional parts differ and are not covered by this calculation.

title: Image Filter is Filter
theorem_text:
Let $X, Y$ be sets.
Let $\mathcal P \left({X}\right)$ and $\mathcal P \left({Y}\right)$ be the power sets of $X$ and $Y$ respectively.
Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping.
Let $\mathcal F \subset \mathcal P \left({X}\right)$ be a filter on $X$.
Then the image filter of $\mathcal F$ with respect to $f$:
$f \left[{\mathcal F}\right] := \left\{ {U \subseteq Y: f^{-1} \left[{U}\right] \in \mathcal F}\right\}$
is a filter on $Y$.
proof_text:
From the definition of a filter we have to prove four things:
$(1): \quad f \left[{\mathcal F}\right] \subset \mathcal P \left({Y}\right)$
$(2): \quad Y \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right], \varnothing \notin f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$
$(3): \quad U, V \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right] \implies U \cap V \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$
$(4): \quad U \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right], U \subseteq V \subseteq Y \implies V \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$
By construction we have:
$f \left[{\mathcal F}\right] \subseteq \mathcal P \left({Y}\right)$
Since $f^{-1} \left[{\varnothing}\right] = \varnothing \notin \mathcal F$ we know that:
$\varnothing \notin f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$
Therefore:
$f \left[{\mathcal F}\right] \ne \mathcal P \left({Y}\right)$
which implies $(1)$.
Because $f^{-1} \left[{Y}\right] = X \in \mathcal F$, we have:
$Y \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$
Since we've already shown $\varnothing \notin f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$, this implies $(2)$.
Let $U, V \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$.
From Preimage of Intersection under Mapping:
$f^{-1} \left[{U \cap V}\right] = f^{-1} \left[{U}\right] \cap f^{-1} \left[{V}\right] \in \mathcal F$
(since $\mathcal F$ is a filter).
Thus $U \cap V \in f \left[{\mathcal F}\right]$, and so $(3)$ holds.
We have established the properness and intersection conditions. This gives a filter on $Y$.
review_reason: The proof never verifies upward closure. To establish it one must show that U contained in V transfers to containment of their preimages and then use the original filter's upward closure.

title: Image of Ultrafilter is Ultrafilter
theorem_text:
Let $X, Y$ be two sets, $f: X \to Y$ a mapping and $\mathcal F$ an ultrafilter on $X$.
Then the image filter $f \left({\mathcal F}\right)$ is an ultrafilter on $Y$.
proof_text: Take $f$ to be a bijection. Its preimage map then gives an inclusion-preserving bijection of the two power sets and respects intersections. Any proper enlargement of $f(\mathcal F)$ to a filter on $Y$ would transport back to a proper enlargement of $\mathcal F$ on $X$, contradicting maximality.
review_reason: The argument uses an inverse correspondence of power sets that requires f to be a bijection. Only a mapping is given, so noninjective and nonsurjective maps remain untreated.

title: Wallis's Product
theorem_text:
$$\prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {2 n} {2 n - 1} \cdot \frac {2 n} {2 n + 1} = \frac 2 1 \cdot \frac 2 3 \cdot \frac 4 3 \cdot \frac 4 5 \cdot \frac 6 5 \cdot \frac 6 7 \cdot \frac 8 7 \cdot \frac 8 9 \cdots$$
$$= \frac \pi 2$$
proof_text:
From the Reduction Formula for Integral of Power of Sine, we have:
$\displaystyle (1): \quad \int \sin^n x \rd x = - \frac 1 n \sin^{n - 1} \cos x + \frac {n - 1} n \int \sin^{n - 2} x \rd x$
Let $I_n$ be defined as:
$\displaystyle I_n = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin^n x \rd x$
As $\cos \dfrac \pi 2 = 0$ from Shape of Cosine Function, we have from $(1)$ that:
$(2): \quad I_n = \dfrac {n-1} n I_{n-2}$
To start the ball rolling, we note that:
$\displaystyle I_0 = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \rd x = \frac \pi 2 \qquad \qquad I_1 = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin x \rd x = \left[{- \cos x}\right]_0^{\pi / 2} = 1$
We need to separate the cases where the subscripts are even and odd:
$$I_{2 n} = \frac {2 n - 1} {2 n} I_{2 n - 2}$$
$$= \frac {2 n - 1} {2 n} \cdot \frac {2 n - 3} {2 n - 2} I_{2 n - 4}$$
$$= \cdots$$
$$= \frac {2 n - 1} {2 n} \cdot \frac {2 n - 3} {2 n - 2} \cdot \frac {2 n - 5} {2 n - 4} \cdots \frac 3 4 \cdot \frac 1 2 I_0$$
(A) $$= \frac {2 n - 1} {2 n} \cdot \frac {2 n - 3} {2 n - 2} \cdot \frac {2 n - 5} {2 n - 4} \cdots \frac 3 4 \cdot \frac 1 2 \cdot \frac \pi 2$$
$$I_{2 n+1} = \frac {2 n} {2 n + 1} I_{2 n - 1}$$
$$= \frac {2 n} {2 n + 1} \cdot \frac {2 n - 2} {2 n - 1} I_{2 n - 3}$$
$$= \cdots$$
$$= \frac {2 n} {2 n + 1} \cdot \frac {2 n - 2} {2 n - 1} \cdot \frac {2 n - 4} {2 n - 3} \cdots \frac 4 5 \cdot \frac 2 3 I_1$$
(B) $$= \frac {2 n} {2 n + 1} \cdot \frac {2 n - 2} {2 n - 1} \cdot \frac {2 n - 4} {2 n - 3} \cdots \frac 4 5 \cdot \frac 2 3$$
From these two product formulas we use the limiting value of the ratio of the even and odd integrals.
Now we take $(B)$ and divide it by $(A)$ to get:
$\dfrac {I_{2 n + 1} } {I_{2 n} } = \dfrac 2 1 \cdot \dfrac 2 3 \cdot \dfrac 4 3 \cdot \dfrac 4 5 \cdots \dfrac {2 n} {2 n - 1} \cdot \dfrac {2 n} {2 n + 1} \cdot \dfrac 2 \pi$
So:
$\dfrac \pi 2 = \dfrac 2 1 \cdot \dfrac 2 3 \cdot \dfrac 4 3 \cdot \dfrac 4 5 \cdots \dfrac {2 n} {2 n - 1} \cdot \dfrac {2 n} {2 n + 1} \cdot \left({\dfrac {I_{2 n} } {I_{2 n + 1} } }\right)$
Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$ gives the result.
review_reason: The finite product identities survive, but the proof removes the bounds establishing that the ratio of the even and odd integrals tends to 1. That limit is needed for the final infinite product value.

title: Binomial Coefficient involving Prime
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Let $\dbinom n p$ be a binomial coefficient.
Then:
$\dbinom n p \equiv \floor {\dfrac n p} \pmod p$
where:
$\floor {\dfrac n p}$
denotes the floor function.
proof_text:
Follows directly from Lucas' Theorem:
$\dbinom n k \equiv \dbinom {\floor {n / p} } {\floor {k / p} } \dbinom {n \bmod p} {k \bmod p} \pmod p$
where $k = p$.
Then:
$k\bmod p=1$.
and so by Binomial Coefficient with Zero:
$\dbinom {n \bmod p} {k \bmod p} = 1$
Also:
$\floor {k / p} = 1$
and by Binomial Coefficient with One:
$\dbinom {\floor {n / p} } {\floor {k / p} } = \floor {\dfrac n p}$
Thus:
$\dbinom n p \equiv \floor {\dfrac n p} \times 1 \pmod p$
Hence the result.
review_reason: The calculation sets k=p, whose remainder on division by p is 0. The altered remainder also makes the following use of the zero lower index inconsistent.

title: Binomial Coefficient of Prime Minus One Modulo Prime
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Then:
$0 \le k \le p - 1 \implies \dbinom {p - 1} k \equiv \left({-1}\right)^k \pmod p$
where $\dbinom {p - 1} k$ denotes a binomial coefficient.
proof_text:
From Binomial Coefficient of Prime, we have:
$\dbinom p k \equiv 0 \pmod p$
when $1 \le k \le p - 1$.
The initial coefficient is $\binom{p-1}{0}=1$. Therefore the coefficients in row $p-1$ have the asserted alternating signs modulo $p$.
review_reason: Knowing the initial coefficient and the interior residues of row p does not connect successive entries of row p−1. The proof omits the recurrence furnished by Pascal's rule.

title: Binomial Coefficient of Prime Plus One Modulo Prime
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Then:
$2 \le k \le p - 1 \implies \dbinom {p + 1} k \equiv 0 \pmod p$
where $\dbinom {p + 1} k$ denotes a binomial coefficient.
proof_text: By Binomial Coefficient of Prime, every interior binomial coefficient in a prime row is divisible by that row's prime. Apply this to the row of order $p+1$ to establish the desired congruence modulo $p$.
review_reason: The cited result requires the row index to be prime and gives divisibility by that same index. In general p+1 is composite, and the needed modulus is p.

title: Number of Primes is Infinite
theorem_text: The number of primes is infinite.
proof_text: Suppose the primes form a finite list $p_1,\ldots,p_k$. Let $N=p_1\cdots p_k+1$ and take $N$ to be prime. None of the listed primes divides $N$, since its remainder modulo any of them is 1, so $N$ is a new prime. This contradicts finiteness.
review_reason: The product plus one is assumed prime. For the prefix through 13 it equals 30031=59·509. A correct argument uses a prime divisor of N.

title: Quotient and Remainder to Number Base
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z: n > 0$ be an integer.
Let $n$ be expressed in base $b$:
$\displaystyle n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m {r_j b^j}$
i.e.
$n = \left[{r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}\right]_b$
Then:
$\displaystyle \left \lfloor {\frac n b} \right \rfloor = \left[{r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1}\right]_b$
$n \bmod b = r_0$
where:
$\left \lfloor {.} \right \rfloor$ denotes the floor function;
$n \bmod b$ denotes the modulo operation.
proof_text:
From the Quotient-Remainder Theorem, we have:
$\exists q, r \in \Z: n = q b + r$
where $0 \le b < r$.
We have that:
$$n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m {r_j b^j}$$
$$= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^m {r_j b^j} + r_0$$
$$= b\sum_{j=1}^m r_j b^{j-1}-r_0.$$
This has the quotient represented by the higher-place digits and remainder $-r_0$, so gives the stated quotient and remainder.
The result follows from the definition of the modulo operation.
review_reason: Separating the units term retains +r_0. Its sign cannot be reversed, and a negative value is also outside the allowed remainder range when r_0 is positive.

title: Gaussian Integers form Subring of Complex Numbers
theorem_text:
The ring of Gaussian integers:
$\struct {\Z \sqbrk i, +, \times}$
forms a subring of the set of complex numbers $\C$.
proof_text:
From Complex Numbers form Field, $\C$ forms a field.
By definition, a field is a ring.
Thus it is possible to use the Subring Test.
We note that $\Z \sqbrk i$ is not empty, as (for example) $0 + 0 i \in \Z \sqbrk i$.
Let $a + b i, c + d i \in \Z \sqbrk i$.
Then we have $-\paren {c + d i} = -c - d i$, and so:
$$\paren {a + b i} + \paren {-\paren {c + d i} } = \paren {a + b i} + \paren {- c - d i}$$
$$= \paren {a + \paren {-c} } + \paren {b + \paren {-d} } i$$
$$= \paren {a - c} + \paren {b - d} i$$
We have that $a, b, c, d \in \Z$ and $\Z$ is an integral domain, therefore by definition a ring.
So it follows that $a - c \in \Z$ and $b - d \in \Z$, and hence:
$\paren {a - c} + \paren {b - d} i \in \Z \sqbrk i$
Thus the Gaussian integers are nonempty and closed under subtraction. The Subring Test gives the conclusion.
So by the Subring Test, $\Z \sqbrk i$ is a subring of $\C$.
review_reason: The proof omits closure under multiplication. A nonempty subset closed under differences satisfies only the additive part of the subring test.

title: Complex Conjugation is Automorphism
theorem_text:
Consider the field of complex numbers $\C$.
The operation of complex conjugation:
$\forall z \in \C: z \mapsto \overline z$
is a field automorphism.
proof_text:
Let $z_1 = x_1 + i y_1, z_2 = x_2 + i y_2$.
Let us define the mapping $\phi: \C \to \C$ defined as:
$\forall z \in \C: \map \phi z = \overline z$
We check that $\phi$ has the morphism property:
By Sum of Complex Conjugates:
$\map \phi {z_1 + z_2} = \map \phi {z_1} + \map \phi {z_2}$
This is the required additive identity.
Hence we can say that complex conjugation is a field homomorphism.
We note that $\overline z_1 = \overline z_2 \implies z_1 = z_2$ and so complex conjugation is injective.
Also, complex conjugation is trivially surjective, and hence bijective.
The result then follows by definition of field automorphism.
review_reason: The map is shown to preserve addition and to be bijective. The proof removes verification of preservation of multiplication, which is essential for a field automorphism.

title: Ring of Sets is Semiring of Sets
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R$ be a ring of sets.
Then $\mathcal R$ is also a semiring of sets.
proof_text:
Let $A \in \mathcal R$.
Suppose $A_1 \subseteq A$.
Let $A_2 = A \setminus A_1$, where $A \setminus A_1$ denotes set difference.
By definition, $A_2$ is then the relative complement of $A_1$ with respect to $A$.
From Union with Relative Complement it then follows that $A_1 \cup A_2 = A$.
By Ring of Sets Closed under Various Operations:
$A \setminus A_1 = A_2 \in \mathcal R$
But by Set Difference Intersection with Second Set is Empty Set:
$\left({A \setminus A_1}\right) \cap A_1 = \varnothing$
Hence for any given $A$ for which we have $A_1 \subseteq A$, we can represent $A$ as the finite expansion $A_1 \cup A_2$ such that $A_1 \cap A_2 = \varnothing$ and $A_1, A_2 \in \mathcal R$
Thus, by definition, $\mathcal R$ is a semiring of sets.
review_reason: Difference closure needs A1 to be a member of the ring as well as a subset of A. The proof asserts membership of A1 and its complement for every subset, which need not hold.

title: Ring of Sets Closed under Finite Intersection
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R$ be a ring of sets.
Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n \in \mathcal R$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \bigcap_{j \mathop = 1}^n A_j \in \mathcal R$
proof_text: Take $\mathcal R$ to be totally ordered by inclusion. Among the finitely many members $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ there is a least one, say $A_k$. Their intersection equals $A_k$, so it is in $\mathcal R$.
review_reason: The proof assumes the ring is a chain for inclusion. The power set of a two-element set is a ring containing incomparable singleton members.

title: Addition Law of Probability
theorem_text: $\map \Pr {A \cup B} = \map \Pr A + \map \Pr B - \map \Pr {A \cap B}$
proof_text:
By definition, a probability measure is a measure.
Apply countable additivity directly to the sequence of events $A,B,\varnothing,\ldots$. This gives $\Pr(A\cup B)=\Pr(A)+\Pr(B)$ and proves the addition law.
review_reason: Countable additivity requires pairwise disjoint events. The statement allows overlap, for example A=B equal to the whole space, when this calculation counts its probability twice.

title: Addition Law of Probability
theorem_text: $\map \Pr {A \cup B} = \map \Pr A + \map \Pr B - \map \Pr {A \cap B}$
proof_text:
From Set Difference and Intersection form Partition:
$A$ is the union of the two disjoint sets $A \setminus B$ and $A \cap B$
$B$ is the union of the two disjoint sets $B \setminus A$ and $A \cap B$.
So, by the definition of probability measure:
$\map \Pr A = \map \Pr {A \setminus B} + \map \Pr {A \cap B}$
$\map \Pr B = \map \Pr {B \setminus A} + \map \Pr {A \cap B}$
From Set Difference is Disjoint with Reverse:
$\paren {A \setminus B} \cap \paren {B \setminus A} = \O$
Hence:
$$\map\Pr A+\map\Pr B=\map\Pr{A\setminus B}+\map\Pr{A\cap B}+\map\Pr{B\setminus A}.$$
$$= \map \Pr {\paren {A \setminus B} \cup \paren {A \cap B} \cup \paren {B \setminus A} } + \map \Pr {A \cap B}$$
Set Difference and Intersection form Partition: Corollary 1
$$= \map \Pr {A \cup B} + \map \Pr {A \cap B}$$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Adding the two preceding partition identities counts the intersection twice. The modified line loses one copy, so it cannot justify the subsequent regrouping.

title: Finite Union of Sets in Additive Function
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal A$ be an algebra of sets.
Let $f: \mathcal A \to \overline {\R}$ be an additive function.
Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be any finite collection of pairwise disjoint elements of $\mathcal A$.
Then:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i}\right) = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n f \left({A_i}\right)$
That is, for any collection of pairwise disjoint elements of $\mathcal A$, $f$ of their union equals the sum of $f$ of the individual elements.
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
In the below, we assume that $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ are all pairwise disjoint elements of $\mathcal A$.
For all $n \in \N_{>0}$, let $P \left({n}\right)$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i}\right) = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n f \left({A_i}\right)$
$P(1)$ is true, as this just says:
$f \left({A_1}\right) = f \left({A_1}\right)$
Basis for the Induction
$P(2)$ is the case:
$f \left({A_1 \cup A_2}\right) = f \left({A_1}\right) + f \left({A_2}\right)$
which comes from the definition of an additive function.
This is our basis for the induction.
Pad the finite family of sets with empty sets to obtain a disjoint sequence. Apply countable additivity of $f$ to that sequence. The empty sets contribute 0, leaving precisely the claimed finite sum.
review_reason: The hypothesis provides only finite additivity, and the argument cites countable additivity without establishing its hypothesis. The binary-additivity induction needed here has been removed.

title: Finite Union of Sets in Subadditive Function
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal A$ be an algebra of sets.
Let $f: \mathcal A \to \overline {\R}$ be a subadditive function.
Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be any finite collection of elements of $\mathcal A$.
Then:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i}\right) \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n f \left({A_i}\right)$
That is, for any finite collection of elements of $\mathcal A$, $f$ of their union is less than or equal to the sum of $f$ of the individual elements.
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
In the below, we assume that $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ are all elements of $\mathcal A$.
For all $n \in \N_{>0}$, let $P \left({n}\right)$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i}\right) \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n f \left({A_i}\right)$
$P(1)$ is trivially true, as this just says $f \left({A_1}\right) \le f \left({A_1}\right)$.
Basis for the Induction
$P(2)$ is the case $f \left({A_1 \cup A_2}\right) \le f \left({A_1}\right) + f \left({A_2}\right)$, which comes from the definition of a subadditive function.
This is our basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $P \left({k}\right)$ is true, where $k \ge 2$, then it logically follows that $P \left({k+1}\right)$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^k A_i}\right) \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k f \left({A_i}\right)$
Then we need to show:
$\displaystyle f \left({\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^{k+1} A_i}\right) \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k+1} f \left({A_i}\right)$
Apply the theorem on countable subadditivity by appending empty sets to $A_1,\ldots,A_n$. The value on the union is at most the series of values on the sequence. Dropping the empty terms gives the required bound.
review_reason: The given subadditivity concerns two sets. The countable inequality and the zero value on the empty set cannot be invoked from that hypothesis without further justification.

title: Additive Function on Empty Set is Zero
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal A$ be an algebra of sets.
Let $f: \mathcal A \to \overline {\R}$ be an additive function on $\mathcal A$.
Then $f \left({\varnothing}\right) = 0$.
proof_text:
First we check that the statement of the theorem makes sense.
And we have that from Properties of Algebras of Sets we have that $\varnothing \in \mathcal A$.
Now let $X \in \mathcal A$.
From Intersection with Empty Set we have that $X \cap \varnothing = \varnothing$, and so $X$ and $\varnothing$ are disjoint.
As $f$ is additive, it follows by definition that:
$f \left({X \cup \varnothing}\right) = f \left({X}\right) + f \left({\varnothing}\right)$
But $X \cup \varnothing = X$ from Union with Empty Set and so:
$f \left({X}\right) = f \left({X}\right) + f \left({\varnothing}\right)$
Hence the result:
$f \left({\varnothing}\right) = 0$
review_reason: The cancellation of f(X) is invalid if f(X) is infinite. With the stated extended-real codomain the identically positive-infinite function obeys binary disjoint additivity.

title: Additive Function is Strongly Additive
theorem_text:
Let $\SS$ be an algebra of sets.
Let $f: \SS \to \overline \R$ be an additive function on $\SS$.
Then $f$ is also strongly additive.
That is:
$\forall A, B \in \SS: \map f {A \cup B} + \map f {A \cap B} = \map f A + \map f B$
proof_text:
For any $A$ and $B$ apply inclusion–exclusion for probability measures. Rearranging that formula gives
$$ f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)=f(A)+f(B).$$
Hence the additive function is strongly additive.
review_reason: The invoked probability theorem requires a probability measure, while f is only finitely additive and may take extended real values. This citation does not cover the given function.
